rationale: Boncompagni §2.1 defines an induced subgraph as the graph obtained by retaining a vertex set with all edges between it and defines containment up to an isomorphic induced subgraph. The item recasts that clause as an injective adjacency-and-nonadjacency preserving map and names its image, so the statement is ai-altered with semantic-source evidence. There is no proof component.

Boncompagni §2.1 supplies the induced-subgraph and isomorphic-copy clauses from which transitivity follows, but it does not state composition of induced embeddings in the library's map notation. The statement is therefore an AI reformulation, and the numbered composition check is locally generated from the two biconditionals.

Kopparty's Local Structure notes define Ind(F,G) for induced copies and ind(F,G) as its cardinality. The item instead counts labelled injective induced embeddings and explains the multiplicity contributed by one image, a material convention change, so the source is semantic rather than exact. There is no proof component.

Kopparty's Ind(F,G)/ind(F,G) clause supplies the induced-copy counting concept, while the library statement adds invariance under relabelling and simultaneous complementation for its labelled-embedding convention. Those equalities and their bijections are locally formulated and proved, giving ai-altered statement and ai-generated proof.

Boncompagni §2.1 says that G contains H when an induced subgraph of G is isomorphic to H, defines H-free by absence of such a copy, and defines family-freeness by requiring H-freeness for every H in the family. Those hypotheses, quantifiers, and the induced convention match the item; the zero-count display is only the library's notation for the same condition. The statement is literature-derived with exact-source evidence, and there is no proof component.

Boncompagni's H-free/family-free clause and its definition of hereditary closure identify induced-subgraph closure as the relevant operation. The specific transitivity lemma is not quoted there; the library states it in its own embedding notation and supplies a local contradiction proof, so both components remain AI-authored adaptations.

Boncompagni §2.1 defines a hereditary class as one closed under induced subgraphs and states that it contains every isomorphic copy of each member. This is exactly the item's two-clause definition under the same finite-graph convention, with only the induced-embedding notation unpacked. The statement is literature-derived/exact-source and has no proof component.

Boncompagni §2.1 defines family-freeness and hereditary closure, and later represents hereditary classes by forbidden induced subgraphs. The item isolates the forward closure implication as a lemma and proves it by composing induced copies; that formulation and numbered proof are local, so the evidence is semantic-source.

Boncompagni §2.1 specifies the forbidden family for a hereditary class as graphs outside the class whose every proper induced subgraph lies inside it, alongside the family-free characterization. This matches the item's minimal-forbidden and forbidden-basis clauses, including induced rather than arbitrary subgraphs; notation and cross-references are editorial. The statement is literature-derived/exact-source and has no proof component.

Boncompagni's clause that every hereditary class is F-free for the family of outside graphs minimal under proper induced subgraphs supplies the existence direction. The item strengthens the presentation to an explicit iff, minimality inside any other basis, and uniqueness up to isomorphism; its minimal-counterexample proof is local, so statement and proof are semantic adaptations rather than an exact recovery.

Boncompagni defines hereditary classes by closure under vertex deletion/induced subgraphs. The null-graph consequence is not separately stated in the cited clause and depends on the library's empty-graph convention; the item and its one-step deletion argument are locally generated from that source concept.

The ISGCI self-complementary-classes page uses co-class/complement-class relationships among named graph classes. It does not state the item's set-builder definition, isomorphism-closure qualification, or warning against set-theoretic complement, so the statement is an AI-authored formalization supported only semantically. There is no proof component.

Diestel Chapter 1 separately defines graph complementation and induced subgraphs on a chosen vertex set. The identity between complementing before or after induction is a local synthesis of those clauses, and the edge-by-edge biconditional proof is locally written; hence ai-altered/ai-generated with semantic-source evidence.

Boncompagni supplies induced-subgraph closure and minimal forbidden families, while the ISGCI page supplies complement-class usage. Neither source states the combined theorem mapping hereditary classes and their minimal bases under complementation; the statement and numbered argument are local adaptations of those clauses.

Boncompagni's induced H-free clause and the ISGCI complement-class convention together support the adjacency/nonadjacency swap used here. The displayed equivalence for arbitrary G and H and its embedding-composition proof are formulated locally, so both components are AI-authored semantic derivations.

Boncompagni explicitly defines a clique as a pairwise adjacent vertex set, a stable set as a pairwise nonadjacent set, and introduces the clique number. The item additionally bundles the stability number, empty-set convention, existence of both maxima, and values on K0, so it materially extends the cited clause and remains ai-altered/semantic-source. There is no proof component.

Boncompagni's clique/stable-set definitions give the pairwise adjacency clauses, and the ISGCI complement-class page supplies the complementation convention. The omega/alpha equalities are not stated as such in those references; the library derives them locally by swapping adjacency with nonadjacency.

Boncompagni defines anticonnected to mean that the complement is connected and an anticomponent as a maximal anticonnected induced subgraph, equivalently a component of the complement. The item adds the co-connected alias, vertex-set formulation, and explicit null/singleton convention, so it is a semantic adaptation rather than exact-source. There is no proof component.

Boncompagni's anticomponent clause explicitly identifies anticomponents with connected components of the complement. The item repackages that clause as a lemma and adds the partition consequence; its short verification is written locally in the library's dependency format.

The Princeton cographs survey states that every non-null graph with at least two vertices is connected or anticonnected. The item specializes this to the library's finite-graph and null-graph conventions and adds an equivalent disconnected-complement formulation; the cross-edge proof is locally written, so the recovery is semantic rather than exact.

Boncompagni defines disjoint vertex sets as complete or anticomplete according as all or no cross-pairs are adjacent. The item adds an edge-between-sets definition, the pure/mixed umbrella terms, and the vacuous empty-set convention, none of which is supplied by that clause; it is therefore ai-altered/semantic-source with no proof component.

Boncompagni supplies the complete/anticomplete cross-pair clauses and the ISGCI page supplies graph complementation. The symmetry, complement swap, and pure/mixed invariance are bundled and proved locally rather than quoted from either source, so statement and proof are AI adaptations.

Boncompagni states that distinct anticomponents are complete to one another and defines components/anticomponents through connectivity and complement connectivity. The item combines that sourced anticomponent clause with the dual component clause and gives its own path and complement proof, so the result is semantic-source rather than an exact transcription.

Diestel §1.1 explicitly distinguishes a subgraph from an induced subgraph and Figure 1.1.3 exhibits a subgraph that is not induced. The local K3 with a P3 edge-subgraph is a new concrete witness to that distinction; it does not attribute the false converse to Diestel. The construction and numbered check are locally generated from the sourced distinction.

Kopparty defines induced-copy counts through Ind(F,G) and ind(F,G). The item converts that framework to the library's labelled-embedding convention and computes two orientations for every edge, so the formula 2|E(G)| and its counting verification are local semantic adaptations.

Boncompagni's H-free and hereditary clauses imply that forbidding the two-vertex stable graph describes complete graphs and that the class is induced-subgraph closed. The particular basis identification and verification are locally formulated from those clauses, so both components are AI-authored semantic derivations.

Boncompagni's forbidden-induced-subgraph definition and the ISGCI complement-class convention identify the complement-dual of complete graphs. The K2-free description of edgeless graphs and its local verification are not copied from either page, so the statement is ai-altered and the proof ai-generated.

The ISGCI Cluster graphs page states both that cluster graphs are disjoint unions of cliques and that they are exactly the P3-free graphs. The item retains that equivalence but expands it into the library's finite-component conventions and supplies its own two-direction proof, making the statement semantic-source and the proof locally generated.

Boncompagni defines hereditary closure specifically under induced subgraphs. The local P3 witness tests that clause: deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices and destroys connectedness. The source is used only for the closure criterion; the counterexample construction and verification are locally generated.

Boncompagni's hereditary clause requires every induced subgraph of a member to remain in the class. The local C4 witness violates that requirement because a three-vertex induced path has degrees 1,2,1; no claim that regular graphs are hereditary is attributed to the source. The construction and degree check are local.

The Princeton cographs survey uses P4 as a graph whose connectedness and complement-connectedness realize the connected/anticonnected dichotomy. The item fixes labels, exhibits the complement path explicitly, and verifies both properties locally, so its construction is a semantic adaptation with an AI-generated check.

Boncompagni's complete/anticomplete cross-set clauses supply the tests used on vertex subsets. The chosen pairs inside a labelled P4 and their pure/mixed classification are library-created examples, and the cross-edge enumeration is locally generated.

Boncompagni states that the minimal forbidden family for a hereditary class consists of all outside graphs whose proper induced subgraphs lie inside; it does not assert that this family is finite. Diestel's cycle definitions support the local infinite family of odd-cycle obstructions. The item refutes the added finiteness claim using a locally written witness family rather than presenting it as sourced truth.

Boncompagni's definition says hereditary classes are closed under induced subgraphs, not under arbitrary edge-deleted subgraphs. The local example takes K3 in the class of complete graphs and deletes one edge to obtain P3, directly exposing the omitted word induced; the refutation is locally generated.

Boncompagni supplies forbidden induced-subgraph bases and the ISGCI page supplies complement-class usage. The paired K2/two-isolated-vertices bases for complete and edgeless graphs are a concrete local instantiation of those clauses, with the verification derived in the item rather than copied.

Diestel Chapter 1 §1.5 defines a forest as an acyclic graph, a tree as a connected forest, and degree-one vertices as leaves. Those are exactly the item's defining clauses under the same finite simple graph convention; the K1 and nontrivial-tree sentences merely spell out the shared degree convention. The statement is literature-derived/exact-source and has no proof component.

Diestel §1.5 supplies the forest/tree/leaf clauses, and the ISI Trees section uses the standard leaf structure of finite trees. The item states the low-degree result for possibly disconnected forests and proves it by a locally chosen longest path, so the statement and proof are semantic adaptations.

The ISI Trees section states the tree edge count and builds forests from tree components. The item promotes this to the exact formula |E(F)|=|V(F)|-c(F) for arbitrary finite forests and proves it by induction; that formulation and proof are local, so the source support is semantic.

The ISI Trees section states that a tree on n vertices has n-1 edges. The item's finite-cardinality notation follows that clause, but its derivation as the one-component case of the local forest theorem is not the sourced proof; statement is ai-altered and proof ai-generated.

Diestel §1.5 states the minimal-connectivity characterization of trees: deleting any edge disconnects a tree, alongside acyclicity. The item adds the exact two-component conclusion and that both components are trees, then proves those refinements locally, so semantic-source is the appropriate evidence.

Diestel Theorem 1.5.1 gives the maximally acyclic characterization of a tree: adding any missing edge creates a cycle, and the unique-path characterization identifies that cycle. The item combines these clauses into an exact-one-cycle lemma and proves uniqueness locally. The former unused edge-deletion fact has been removed, so the recorded derivation now matches the proof actually given.

Diestel Theorem 1.5.1 states the unique-path, minimal-connectivity, and maximal-acyclic tree characterizations, while Corollary 1.5.2 supplies the n-1 edge tests. The item combines those sourced results into one six-way finite-graph theorem and adapts the proof to local prerequisites, hence both statement and proof are ai-altered with semantic-source evidence.

The ISI Trees section states the standard leaf conclusion for nontrivial finite trees. The library restates it under its degree-one/K1 convention and supplies its own longest-path proof, so the statement is a semantic adaptation and the proof locally generated.

Diestel §1.5 defines a rooted tree by choosing a root, introduces the root-induced tree order, and identifies level sets. The item replaces the order language with root paths, depth, height, ancestor, parent, and child terminology, materially bundling additional clauses; it is therefore ai-altered/semantic-source with no proof component.

Diestel's rooted-tree paragraph supplies the root order and level partition. The item translates those notions into parent uniqueness, depth increments, and level partition statements and proves them from unique paths; those formulations and the numbered proof are local semantic adaptations.

Diestel §1.5 defines a spanning tree of G as a spanning subgraph that is a tree. This matches the item's definition and equivalent vertex/edge conditions under the same conventions; the null-graph sentence only makes the shared nonempty connected-tree convention explicit. The statement is literature-derived/exact-source and has no proof component.

Diestel's proof that every connected graph has a spanning tree takes a maximal acyclic spanning subgraph and shows that disconnected components would admit another edge. The item isolates that proof step as a lemma and rewrites it in the library's maximality notation; statement and numbered proof are adapted rather than copied exactly.

Diestel Corollary 1.5.3 states that a graph is connected if and only if it has a spanning tree. The item preserves the equivalence but supplies a local finite-edge maximality proof and an explicit reverse implication, so the statement is source-based but reformatted and the proof is locally generated.

Diestel §1.5 states that every chord of a spanning tree determines a unique fundamental cycle, consisting of the chord and the tree path between its endpoints. The item restates that clause in T+e notation and supplies its own proof from unique paths, so semantic-source and ai-generated proof are appropriate.

Diestel §1.5 defines the fundamental cut associated with a tree edge and its two components. The item adds the exchange conclusion for every graph edge crossing that cut and proves connectivity and acyclicity locally. The unused tree-characterization fact has been removed, leaving only the edge-deletion and spanning clauses actually used.

Diestel's spanning-tree definition identifies every spanning tree with an edge subset of a finite graph. The item turns that observation into an explicit finiteness lemma and proves injection into the finite power set locally, so it is a semantic consequence rather than an exact sourced result.

The ISI Trees section introduces the number of spanning trees of a graph and the standard notation for that count. This matches the item's cardinality definition under the same finite-graph convention; the zero case only expands the meaning of an empty counted set. The statement is literature-derived/exact-source and has no proof component.

The ISI Prüfer-code section gives the repeated least-leaf deletion algorithm and records its neighbour until two labels remain. The item generalizes from the source's standard label set to an arbitrary finite subset of natural labels and includes a termination/well-definedness argument, so the statement is materially adapted and only semantically sourced. There is no separate proof component.

The ISI Prüfer-code section gives the inverse decoding construction that repeatedly joins the least absent label and finishes with the last edge. The item adapts that algorithm to arbitrary finite natural label sets and proves its invariants in numbered form, so both statement and proof are ai-altered rather than exact.

The ISI section states the bijection between labelled trees and Prüfer words and explains encoding/decoding as inverses. The item carries the theorem to its arbitrary-subset convention and expands the inverse argument into local numbered steps; both components therefore follow the source semantically but are materially adapted.

The ISI Trees section states Cayley's formula that the number of labelled trees on n vertices is n^(n-2), derived through Prüfer codes. The item translates the result to the library's zero-based label convention and supplies a locally structured bijection/counting proof, so statement and proof remain ai-altered/semantic-source.

ISI §4.3 defines weighted graphs, total spanning-tree weight, and an MST as a spanning tree of least weight. The item changes the source convention to arbitrary real edge weights, adds connected/disconnected existence clauses, and cites local finite-set machinery, so it is a material semantic adaptation with no proof component.

ISI Proposition 4.18 uses the fundamental cycle exchange T+e-f in its MST argument, and its cut discussion supplies the dual crossing-edge exchange. The item extracts both operations as a general two-part spanning-tree lemma and adapts the proof to local fundamental-cycle/cut results; both components are ai-altered.

ISI Proposition 4.18 states cut and cycle properties for minimum spanning trees and proves them by exchanging edges. The item separates tie and unique-weight cases into four quantified clauses and rewrites the exchange argument in the library's notation, so statement and proof are materially adapted from that source.

ISI Proposition 4.18 states uniqueness when the edge-weight function is injective. The item expresses that hypothesis as pairwise distinct real weights and gives a symmetric-difference exchange proof rather than relying on the sourced cut clause. The unused cut-property fact has been removed; the remaining proof is an ai-altered sourced argument.

ISI §4.4 gives Kruskal's increasing-weight, cycle-avoiding algorithm and proves that its output is an MST. The item permits arbitrary tie breaking, formalizes the stopping condition, and adapts the proof to local cut/exchange lemmas, so both components are ai-altered with semantic-source evidence.

ISI §4.4 gives the Jarník/Prim procedure of repeatedly taking a cheapest edge out of the reached vertex set and proves MST correctness. The item restates it with arbitrary tie breaking and rewrites the invariant proof using the local cut property, so statement and proof are semantic adaptations.

Diestel Chapter 1 supplies the tree, degree, path, and star structures used to classify small trees, but it does not give this exact illustrated 1,1,1,2,3 catalogue. The representatives and degree-sequence exhaustion are locally assembled and verified, so the example construction is ai-altered and its proof ai-generated.

The ISI Prüfer section supplies the least-leaf encoding and inverse decoding algorithms. The labelled five-vertex tree, code (2,2,2), drawing, and step-by-step round trip are local choices, so the example and verification are AI-generated adaptations supported semantically by the algorithm clause.

Diestel's spanning-tree and cycle definitions imply that deleting any one edge of Cn gives a path and that every spanning tree must omit an edge. The exact count n, illustration, and two-sided local verification are constructed in the item rather than stated by the cited chapter.

The ISI Cayley theorem counts labelled trees on four vertices as 4^2. The item specializes that clause to K4 and supplies a local Prüfer-word count and drawing, so its example statement is a semantic specialization and the verification is locally generated.

Diestel §1.5 defines a chord's fundamental cycle and a tree edge's fundamental cut. The chosen four-vertex graph, the cycle 1-2-3-4-1, and the cut {23,13,14} are local computations illustrating those clauses, with an AI-generated verification.

Diestel's spanning-tree definition and cycle deletion observation support spanning trees obtained from C3. The specific triangle example and enumeration of its three edge deletions are locally formulated and checked rather than copied from a source example.

ISI §4.4 supplies the Kruskal and Prim selection rules. The five-edge weighted graph, the common choice sequence ab,bc,cd, and total weight 6 are a local worked example, and each algorithm trace is generated in the item.

Diestel §1.5 defines a tree as a connected forest, so acyclicity alone omits the connectedness hypothesis. The local graph consisting of two isolated vertices is acyclic but disconnected and therefore not a tree. The reference supports the true definition; the counterexample and its check are locally generated.

Diestel Corollary 1.5.2 states the n-1 edge characterization only together with connectedness or acyclicity. The local graph C3 disjoint union K1 has four vertices and three edges but fails both missing conditions, so it refutes the count-only claim without attributing that false claim to Diestel. The verification is local.

ISI Proposition 4.18 gives uniqueness only when the edge-weight function is injective. The local equal-weight triangle deliberately violates that hypothesis and has three two-edge spanning trees of the same total weight. The source supplies the omitted-condition clause; the witness and its numbered verification are locally generated.

ISI Theorem 4.5 explicitly counts labelled trees on a fixed n-vertex label set via Prüfer words. The item contrasts that clause with the two unlabelled isomorphism types on four vertices, thereby refuting the word unlabelled rather than treating it as sourced content. The comparison and verification are local.

Diestel §1.5 defines chords as edges of G outside a chosen spanning tree and assigns each such chord a fundamental cycle; this directly shows that connected graphs may have edges excluded from a spanning tree. ISI's exchange clause supports replacing one tree edge by a chord. The local triangle witness and refutation are generated from those true clauses, not from the false universal claim.
